summary: Reserves two blocks of Autonomous System numbers for use in examples in RFCs, books, and other documentation, to avoid confusion with real deployed networks. This is an informational document.

plainLanguage.summary: Writers of cookbooks use pretend phone numbers so nobody gets bothered. This sets aside pretend network numbers for examples.

subtitle: Sets aside fake network numbers to prevent confusion in examples

tldr.problem: When RFCs and books use real Autonomous System numbers in examples, people might try to use them in production, causing conflicts and network disruptions.
tldr.mechanism: IANA reserves two blocks of AS numbers (64496-64511 for 16-bit, 65536-65551 for 32-bit) exclusively for documentation and examples.
tldr.outcome: Documentation can safely use these reserved numbers without risk of real-world conflicts, similar to reserved IP ranges and domain names.

today: RFC 5398 is an Informational document that remains the current standard for AS number documentation reservations.

sections.title: The Example Problem
sections.content: RFC authors, textbook writers, and network engineers need to use Autonomous System numbers in examples to explain how BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) and routing work. If they use real AS numbers, someone might copy the example into production, causing conflicts with actual deployed networks. This document reserves specific AS numbers exclusively for documentation use, avoiding the real-world problems that IPv4 and IPv6 address documentation ranges already solved.
sections.plainLanguage: When you write an example about how networks talk to each other, you need to make-up AS numbers so nobody gets confused and wires up your example by mistake.

sections.title: The Reserved Blocks
sections.content: IANA reserves two blocks of 16 contiguous AS numbers. One block lies in the 16-bit AS number range: 64496 to 64511 (expressions as 16-bit values). The second block is in the 32-bit range: 65536 to 65551 (values that require 32-bit representation). Splitting the reservations allows documentation to show examples of both traditional 16-bit AS numbering and newer 32-bit AS numbering transition scenarios.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two sets of fake AS numbers: one for old-style numbers and one for new-style numbers. Each set has 16 numbers to use in examples.

sections.title: Operational Use
sections.content: BGP routers and operational configurations must never peer with AS numbers from these reserved ranges. This ensures that even if someone accidentally configures documentation examples on live equipment, the reserved AS numbers will not establish real BGP relationships. The reservations are recorded in the IANA AS Number Registry, making them official and universally recognized.
sections.plainLanguage: Real routers should never try to connect to these fake AS numbers, so even if an example accidentally gets configured in production, it will not work.
